title: From Falling Apples to Black Holes
subtitle: What gravity is, what it does, and what nobody knows yet
subject: Physics

pages.h: Everything falls at the same rate
p: Drop a hammer and a feather on the Moon and they hit the ground together. An astronaut, David Scott, did exactly that in 1971, on live television, and the feather did not float. On Earth a feather drifts down only because air pushes on it. Take the air away and every object falls the same way, no matter what it weighs.

Near Earth's surface, a falling object gains 9.8 metres per second of speed every second. After one second it is moving at 9.8 m/s. After two seconds, 19.6 m/s. In the first second alone it drops 4.9 metres, about the height of a giraffe. Scientists write this number as g.

This was a shock when Galileo argued it around 1600. Most people believed heavy things fall faster because that is what it looks like in air. Gravity does pull harder on a heavy thing. But a heavy thing is also harder to get moving. The two effects cancel exactly, and that exact cancelling is one of the deepest clues in all of physics. Hold on to it. It comes back near the end of this book.
pages.cap: A ball speeds up as it rolls down. Gravity adds the same speed every second, whatever the ball is made of.
pages.fact: Did you know? On the Moon, g is only 1.62 m/s2, so a dropped hammer takes 2.5 times longer to land.

pages.h: The Moon is falling right now
p: Isaac Newton's big idea was not that apples fall. Everyone knew that. His idea was that the Moon is falling too, in exactly the same way, and has been falling for four billion years without ever landing.

Here is the trick. The Moon moves sideways at about 1 kilometre per second. Every second, gravity pulls it about 1.4 millimetres toward Earth, off its straight line. But in that same second the Moon has moved so far sideways that the ground has curved away under it by the same 1.4 millimetres. It falls and misses, falls and misses, forever. That is what an orbit is.

Newton checked the numbers. The Moon is 60 times farther from Earth's centre than an apple is. If gravity weakens with the square of distance, the Moon should fall 60 times 60, or 3,600 times, more gently than an apple. It does. One rule, the apple and the Moon. Nobody had ever tied the sky and the ground together with a single equation before.
pages.cap: The Moon is always falling toward Earth and always missing, because it is also moving sideways fast.
pages.fact: Did you know? The Moon takes 27.3 days to fall all the way around us once.

pages.h: The law in one line
p: Newton's law of gravity says every object pulls on every other object. The pull is stronger when the masses are bigger, and weaker when they are farther apart. Double the distance and the pull drops to a quarter. Triple it and the pull drops to a ninth. This is called an inverse square law.

The pull also depends on a tiny number called G, the gravitational constant. It is 0.0000000000667 in standard units. That smallness is why you do not feel your friend pulling on you. Two people a metre apart attract each other with about two ten-millionths of a newton, far less than the weight of a grain of sand.

Earth is different only because it is huge: 5,970,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 kilograms, or 5.97 times ten to the power of 24. Multiply that enormous mass by the tiny G and you get the pull that holds your feet on the floor. Gravity is the weakest force in nature, but it never cancels out and it reaches across all of space. Given enough mass, weak wins.

v.title: Earth has 81 times the Moon's mass

pages.cap: Earth pulls on the Moon and the Moon pulls back on Earth with exactly the same force, just in opposite directions.

pages.h: Weighing the Earth in a shed
p: Nobody could measure G for over a hundred years after Newton, because the pull between ordinary objects is so tiny. Then in 1798 an English scientist named Henry Cavendish built a strange machine in a shed behind his house.

He hung a light wooden rod from a thin wire, with a small lead ball at each end. Near each small ball he placed a big lead ball weighing 158 kilograms. The big balls pulled the small ones ever so slightly, twisting the wire. The twist was so small that Cavendish watched it through a telescope from outside the shed, so that his own body heat would not disturb the air inside.

From that twist he worked out the pull between the balls, and from that, the mass of the whole Earth. His answer was within one percent of the modern value. People say he weighed the Earth, and that is fair. He also showed something quietly amazing: a lump of lead you can hold pulls on another lump of lead, and the pull can be measured.
pages.cap: A balance compares two pulls. Cavendish compared the pull of lead balls with the pull of the whole planet.
pages.fact: Did you know? Earth's average density turned out to be 5.5 times that of water, more than any rock on the surface. That was the first hint of an iron core.

pages.h: You are pulling on the Earth right now
p: Earth pulls you down with a force equal to your weight. You pull Earth up with exactly the same force. Earth barely moves because it has about 100,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 times your mass.

pages.h: Mass is not weight
p: Mass is how much stuff you are made of. It is measured in kilograms, and it is the same everywhere: on Earth, on the Moon, floating in deep space. Weight is the force gravity pulls on that stuff. It changes from place to place.

Take a 50 kilogram person. On Earth, gravity pulls them with a force of about 490 newtons. On the Moon, where g is 1.62 m/s2, the pull is only 81 newtons, about one sixth. On Mars, with g of 3.7 m/s2, it is 185 newtons. On Jupiter, if you could stand on it, g would be 24.8 m/s2 and the pull would be 1,240 newtons, like carrying another person and a half on your back.

Bathroom scales measure force, not mass, so they would read differently on each world. A balance scale that compares you against known kilograms would read the same everywhere, because gravity pulls on both sides equally. When scientists say an astronaut is weightless, they mean no floor is pushing back. The astronaut's mass has not changed one gram.
pages.cap: On the Moon these six children would have the same mass, but each would weigh one sixth of their Earth weight.

pages.q: You drop a 1 kg stone and a 10 kg stone from the same height on the Moon. What happens?
opts: They land at the same time
pages.why: With no air, gravity gives every falling object the same acceleration, so they land together.

pages.h: How to stay in orbit: fall and miss
p: Newton imagined a cannon on a very tall mountain. Fire a ball slowly and it lands nearby. Fire it faster and it lands farther away, because the ground curves away beneath it. Fire it fast enough, about 7.9 kilometres per second near the surface, and the ground curves away exactly as fast as the ball falls. The ball never lands. It is in orbit.
The International Space Station does exactly this, about 400 kilometres up. It travels at 7.7 kilometres per second and circles the planet every 93 minutes. Astronauts see 16 sunrises a day.

Here is the part most people get wrong. Gravity on the station is not zero. At 400 kilometres up it is still about 90 percent as strong as on the ground. The astronauts float because they are falling, together with the station, all the time. A falling elevator would feel the same, for a few seconds. The station just keeps missing the ground. Orbit is not an escape from gravity. It is a very long fall.
pages.cap: The sideways arrow is speed, the inward arrow is gravity. Together they bend the path into a loop.
pages.fact: Did you know? The station loses about 2 kilometres of height each month to thin air drag and needs regular boosts.

pages.h: Why planets move in ovals
p: Orbits are not perfect circles. They are ellipses, slightly squashed circles, and the Sun sits not at the centre but off to one side, at a point called a focus. Johannes Kepler worked this out in 1609 from years of careful planet measurements, before anyone knew why.

Newton's law explains the why. As a planet swings closer to the Sun, gravity pulls harder and the planet speeds up. As it moves away, it slows. The planet trades speed for distance and back again, like a ball rolling into a bowl and out the other side.

Earth's orbit is nearly round. We are closest to the Sun in early January, about 147 million kilometres, and farthest in early July, about 152 million kilometres. That is only a 3 percent difference, which is why winter in Canada is not caused by distance. It is caused by Earth's tilt. Comets are the extreme case. Halley's comet dives to 88 million kilometres from the Sun, then coasts out past Neptune to 5,200 million kilometres, moving slowly, before falling back in. It takes 76 years.
pages.cap: The Sun sits off centre in every planet's orbit. Closer means faster, farther means slower.

pages.h: Try it: measure gravity with a pendulum
p: A swinging weight on a string is a gravity meter. The time for one swing depends only on the string's length and on g.
steps: Tie a small heavy object, like a metal nut or a bunch of keys, to a string exactly 1 metre long from the knot to the middle of the weight.
Hang it from a hook or a door frame so it swings freely without touching anything.
Pull it about 10 centimetres to one side and let go. Do not push.
Use a stopwatch to time 20 full swings (over and back counts as one). Divide by 20 to get the time for one swing, called the period, T.
Calculate g using g = 39.5 x L / (T x T), with L in metres and T in seconds. For L = 1 m, T should be close to 2.0 seconds, giving g close to 9.8 m/s2.
Try a 0.5 m string. The period should drop to about 1.4 seconds, not 1.0. Why?
pages.cap: A one-metre pendulum swings over and back in almost exactly 2 seconds anywhere on Earth.
pages.safe: Keep the swinging weight away from faces and screens.

pages.h: Tides: the Moon stretches the ocean
p: Twice a day the sea rises and falls, and the Moon is the reason. But not in the way most people picture it. The Moon does not simply lift the water beneath it. It stretches the whole Earth.

The side of Earth facing the Moon is about 12,700 kilometres closer than the far side, so it is pulled a little harder. The far side is pulled a little less. The result is two bulges of water, one facing the Moon and one facing away, with low water in between. As Earth spins through both bulges, each place gets two high tides a day, about 12 hours and 25 minutes apart. The extra 25 minutes is because the Moon has moved along its orbit while Earth spun.

The Sun makes tides too, about 46 percent as strong. When Sun and Moon line up, at new moon and full moon, the tides are extra big. These are spring tides, and they have nothing to do with the season. The Bay of Fundy, between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, has the biggest tides on Earth, up to 16 metres, the height of a five-storey building, because the bay's shape makes the water slosh in time with the tide.
pages.cap: At new moon and full moon the Sun and Moon pull along the same line, and tides are at their biggest.
pages.fact: Did you know? The solid ground also has tides. Where you stand rises and falls by about 30 centimetres twice a day.

pages.h: The Moon is drifting away
p: Apollo astronauts left mirrors on the Moon. Scientists still bounce laser beams off them and time the round trip to a few centimetres. The answer is clear: the Moon is moving away from Earth at 3.8 centimetres a year, about the rate your fingernails grow.

Tides are the reason. Earth spins faster than the Moon orbits, so the tidal bulge is dragged slightly ahead of the Moon. That bulge pulls the Moon forward, giving it a tiny boost that lifts it to a higher orbit. In return, the Moon's pull on the bulge acts as a brake on Earth's spin. Our days are getting longer by about 2 milliseconds every century.

Add that up over deep time. About 1.4 billion years ago, a day on Earth lasted only 18 hours, and the Moon looked noticeably bigger in the sky. Growth lines in ancient corals and layers in old tidal mud record this change. In the far future the Moon will be too far away to fully cover the Sun, and total solar eclipses will end. There are still about 600 million years of them left, so there is time.
pages.cap: The Moon formed close to Earth after a giant impact and has been spiralling outward ever since.

pages.h: Escape velocity: how fast is free?
p: Throw a ball up and it comes back. Throw it faster and it goes higher before returning. Is there a speed where it never comes back? Yes. For Earth it is 11.2 kilometres per second, about 40,000 kilometres per hour, and it is called escape velocity.

That number depends on mass and size. Escape the Moon and you need only 2.4 km/s, which is why the lunar lander could take off on a small engine. Escape Jupiter and you need 59.5 km/s. Escape the Sun from its surface: 618 km/s.

Rockets do not actually have to reach 11.2 km/s in one burst. They keep pushing, so they can climb more slowly. But the energy cost is the same, and that is why rockets are mostly fuel. A Falcon 9 at launch is about 95 percent propellant by mass. Only a few percent is the payload that actually goes somewhere.

Now imagine squeezing a body so small and so dense that its escape velocity passes the speed of light, 300,000 km/s. Then nothing could get out, not even light. In 1783 a clergyman named John Michell worked this out using only Newton's rules. He had just described a black hole.
pages.cap: A rocket pushes hot gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up. Most of the rocket is fuel.

pages.q: Why does the Moon slowly move away from Earth?
opts: Earth's tidal bulge tugs the Moon forward and speeds it up
pages.why: Earth spins faster than the Moon orbits, so the tidal bulge sits ahead of the Moon and gives it a tiny forward pull.

pages.h: The planet that broke Newton's law
p: For 200 years Newton's gravity passed every test. It predicted the return of Halley's comet. It found Neptune in 1846 before anyone saw it, from wobbles in the orbit of Uranus. Then it hit a problem with the smallest planet.

Mercury's oval orbit slowly turns, so that its closest point to the Sun drifts around. The other planets' pulls explain most of the turning. But a tiny leftover, 43 arcseconds per century, would not go away. An arcsecond is 1/3,600 of a degree. The error was the width of a coin seen from about 100 metres away, building up over a hundred years. It should have been zero.
Astronomers guessed there was an unseen planet closer to the Sun, and even named it Vulcan. People reported seeing it. None of the sightings held up. For 60 years the mystery sat there.

In 1915 Albert Einstein finished a new theory of gravity and tried it on Mercury. The leftover 43 arcseconds came out of the equations exactly. He later said the result gave him heart palpitations. Newton was not wrong. He was very nearly right, and 'very nearly' had just been measured.
pages.cap: Mercury's oval orbit slowly turns, like a drawing on a plate being rotated. Newton could not explain all of it.

pages.h: Einstein's idea: gravity is not a force
p: Einstein's theory, called general relativity, says something strange. There is no pulling at all. Mass bends space and time together, which physicists call spacetime, and objects simply follow the straightest possible path through the bent shape. Earth does not pull the Moon. Earth bends the space around it, and the Moon rolls along the curve.

Picture a stretched sheet with a bowling ball in the middle. The sheet dips. Roll a marble past and it curves toward the ball, not because the ball grabs it, but because the sheet is sloped. This picture is useful and also a bit of a cheat, because it uses gravity to explain gravity. The real bending is in four dimensions and includes time, and nobody can picture that. Even Einstein needed new mathematics to describe it.

A short way to say the whole theory: matter tells spacetime how to curve, and spacetime tells matter how to move. For slow objects and weak gravity, like apples and planets, the answers match Newton's almost perfectly. For fast things, strong gravity and very precise clocks, the answers differ, and every time we have checked, Einstein's answer has been the right one.
pages.cap: In Einstein's picture a planet is not pulled. It coasts along the straightest line that curved space allows.

pages.h: Falling is floating
p: In 1907 Einstein had what he called the happiest thought of his life. A person falling off a roof would not feel their own weight. While falling, they would float, and if they let go of a ball it would float beside them. Falling and floating in deep space feel identical. You cannot tell them apart from inside a closed box.

Flip it around. Stand in a rocket in deep space, far from any planet, accelerating upward at 9.8 m/s2. You would feel pressed to the floor. Drop a ball and it falls. Everything would feel exactly like standing on Earth. Again, from inside, no experiment can tell the difference.

Einstein took this seriously. If gravity and acceleration cannot be told apart, then gravity is not a special pull. It is what it feels like when the straightest path through curved spacetime is not the path your floor is on. The floor pushes you off that path, and you call the push weight.

Remember the hammer and feather from page one? They fall together because they are not being pulled at all. They are both just following the same curved path. That exact cancelling was the clue all along.
pages.cap: Astronauts on the station are not beyond gravity. They are falling around Earth, so nothing pushes on their feet.

pages.h: Light bends
p: If mass bends space, then light must bend too, even though light has no mass, because it travels through the bent space. Einstein predicted that starlight passing the edge of the Sun would be deflected by 1.75 arcseconds, about the width of a coin seen from 2.5 kilometres. Stars near the Sun should look slightly out of place.

You can only see stars next to the Sun during a total eclipse. In May 1919 two British expeditions, one to the island of Principe off West Africa and one to Sobral in Brazil, photographed the eclipse. The stars had shifted, by about the predicted amount. Einstein became world famous overnight. Scientists have argued since about how precise those first photographs really were, but modern measurements with radio telescopes confirm the number to better than one part in ten thousand.

Today bent light is a tool. A whole galaxy can act as a lens, bending the light of a more distant galaxy behind it into arcs and rings. The James Webb Space Telescope uses these natural lenses to see galaxies so far away that their light has travelled for more than 13 billion years. Gravity, which Newton thought only tugged on things, turns out to be a magnifying glass the size of a galaxy.
pages.cap: A galaxy's gravity bends the light of galaxies behind it, stretching them into arcs and making them brighter.

pages.h: Time runs slower near heavy things
p: Your feet age more slowly than your head, because they are closer to Earth. Over a whole lifetime the difference adds up to about half a millionth of a second. Tiny, but real, and measured with atomic clocks lifted just 33 centimetres.

pages.h: Your phone uses Einstein every day
p: GPS satellites fly 20,200 kilometres up, carrying atomic clocks. Your phone finds its position by timing radio signals from several satellites. Light travels 30 centimetres in a billionth of a second, so a clock error of one billionth of a second means a position error of 30 centimetres.

Two of Einstein's effects pull on those clocks. Up high, where Earth's gravity is weaker, time runs faster. The satellite clocks gain about 45 millionths of a second a day compared with clocks on the ground. But the satellites also move at 3.9 kilometres per second, and moving clocks run slow. That loses about 7 millionths of a second a day. The net result: satellite clocks run fast by 38 millionths of a second every day.

That sounds like nothing. It is not. Thirty-eight millionths of a second of light travel is 11 kilometres. Ignore Einstein and your map app would put you in the wrong town by the end of the first day, and get worse every day after. So engineers set the satellite clocks to tick slightly slow before launch, so they run exactly right once in orbit. Every delivery, every ride-share, every lost hiker found, runs on curved spacetime.
pages.cap: Every map app in every city depends on satellite clocks corrected for gravity's effect on time.
pages.fact: Did you know? The clock in a GPS satellite is set to tick at 10.22999999543 megahertz on the ground so that it reads 10.23 in orbit.

pages.q: Why do astronauts float inside the space station?
opts: There is no gravity 400 km up
They are falling around Earth together with the station
The station's engines hold them up
pages.why: Gravity at the station is still about 90 percent of surface strength. The crew and the station are in free fall together.

pages.h: Ripples in spacetime
p: If spacetime can bend, it can wobble. Einstein predicted in 1916 that moving masses should send out waves in spacetime, stretching and squeezing everything they pass through. He also thought they were far too weak to ever detect.

On 14 September 2015 a detector called LIGO, with two 4-kilometre arms in Louisiana and Washington State, caught one. The signal lasted a fifth of a second and came from two black holes, of 36 and 29 times the Sun's mass, spiralling together and merging 1.3 billion light years away. Three Suns' worth of mass turned into pure gravitational-wave energy. For that fifth of a second, the merger put out more power than all the stars in the visible universe combined.

By the time the waves reached Earth they stretched LIGO's arms by one ten-thousandth of the width of a proton. Measuring that took 40 years of engineering. Three of the leaders received the Nobel Prize in 2017.

In August 2017 detectors caught two neutron stars colliding, 130 million light years away. Telescopes around the world turned to look and saw the flash. In its glowing debris they found the fingerprints of freshly made gold and platinum. More on that story in the chemistry book. Gravity had opened a new kind of eye on the universe.
pages.cap: Two dead stars spiral together. Their crash shakes spacetime and showers out heavy elements.

pages.h: What a black hole really is
p: A black hole is not a hole, and it is not a cosmic vacuum cleaner. It is a place where so much mass is packed into so little space that the escape velocity passes the speed of light. The boundary where that happens is called the event horizon. Cross it and there is no coming back, because nothing can go faster than light.

Any mass has a black hole size. Squeeze the Sun into a ball 6 kilometres across and it would become one. Squeeze Earth to the size of a marble, 18 millimetres across, and it would too. The size is called the Schwarzschild radius, after Karl Schwarzschild, who solved Einstein's equations for it in 1915 while serving as a soldier in the First World War.

From far away, a black hole's gravity is ordinary. If the Sun were replaced by a black hole of the same mass, Earth would keep orbiting exactly as it does now, just in the dark and cold. Black holes do not reach out and grab. Things fall in only if they get close, and most things orbit instead. The strangeness is all packed near the horizon, where space and time swap roles and 'forward in time' points inward.
pages.cap: Gas spiralling toward a black hole heats to millions of degrees and glows. The dark circle in the middle is the shadow of the horizon.

pages.h: The first picture of a black hole
p: In April 2019 scientists showed the world a fuzzy orange ring with a dark centre. It was the first image of a black hole, in the giant galaxy M87, 55 million light years away. The dark patch is the black hole's shadow. The ring is hot gas swirling around it, with light bent by gravity so that we see the far side too.

That black hole has 6.5 billion times the mass of the Sun. Its horizon is about 38 billion kilometres across, wider than our whole solar system. But at that distance it looks as small as an orange on the Moon seen from Earth. No single telescope could see it. So the Event Horizon Telescope team linked radio dishes from Hawaii to Spain to the South Pole, making a virtual telescope the size of Earth, and combined half a tonne of hard drives of data.

In 2022 the same team showed the black hole at the centre of our own galaxy, Sagittarius A star, 27,000 light years away, with 4 million times the Sun's mass. It is far smaller, and the gas around it changes within minutes, which made the picture harder, not easier. Both images matched Einstein's predictions. A century after he wrote the equations, we had photographed the thing they describe.
pages.cap: The ring is brighter on one side because that gas is moving toward us at close to the speed of light.

pages.h: Falling in
p: Suppose you fell into a black hole feet first. Two different stories would be true at the same time, depending on who is watching.

From your point of view, nothing special happens as you cross the horizon. There is no wall, no flash. But gravity is stronger at your feet than at your head, and near a small black hole the difference becomes enormous. You would be stretched longer and squeezed thinner, in a process physicists really do call spaghettification. For a black hole the mass of the Sun this would happen well outside the horizon. For a giant like M87's, you could cross the horizon in one piece and have hours before the stretching began.

From a friend's point of view, watching from a safe distance, you would never cross at all. Near the horizon time runs slower and slower compared with the outside. Your friend would see you slow down, your image getting redder and dimmer, until you seemed to freeze just above the horizon and fade from view. Both stories are correct. Which one you get depends on where you are standing. That is what Einstein meant when he said time is not the same for everyone.
pages.cap: To an outside watcher, a falling object slows, reddens and fades, seeming to freeze forever at the horizon.

pages.h: Try it: curve a sheet and make an orbit
p: This classic model shows why a curved surface makes things go round. It is not how gravity really works, but it shows the idea.
steps: Stretch a large piece of thin stretchy fabric, like a fitted bed sheet or a big piece of spandex, across the top of a box or between four chairs. Clip or tie it tight.
Place a heavy ball, like a bowling ball or a big bag of flour, in the centre. The sheet dips into a bowl shape.
Roll a marble straight across the sheet near the edge. It curves toward the heavy ball. Roll it faster and it curves less.
Now roll the marble sideways at just the right speed. It should circle the ball several times before spiralling in. That spiral is friction, which real planets do not have.
Try two marbles at once and watch them pull toward each other's dips.
Think about what the model gets wrong. The marble is pulled down by real gravity. In the real universe, the bending is in space and time, not a surface below.
pages.cap: A marble circling a dip in a sheet is a toy version of a planet following curved spacetime.
pages.safe: Keep marbles away from small children and pets.

pages.q: If the Sun were suddenly replaced by a black hole of the same mass, what would happen to Earth's orbit?
opts: Earth would fly off into space
Earth would keep orbiting the same way
pages.why: From a distance, gravity depends only on mass. Same mass, same orbit. Earth would just get dark and cold.

pages.h: Why planets are round and mountains are short
p: Every planet and large moon is a ball. Small asteroids are lumpy potatoes. Gravity explains the difference. On a big body, gravity pulls every bulge downward and every hollow fills, until the surface is as even as it can be. Rock may seem rigid, but over millions of years and under enough weight it flows like very thick syrup.

The crossover is around 400 to 600 kilometres across for a rocky body. Vesta, 525 kilometres wide, is lumpy. Ceres, 940 kilometres wide, is round. Ice is softer than rock, so icy moons go round at smaller sizes.

Gravity also sets how tall a mountain can be. Pile rock too high and the base is crushed by the weight above it and spreads out. On Earth the limit is roughly 10 kilometres. Mount Everest stands 8,849 metres. On Mars, where gravity is only 38 percent of Earth's, Olympus Mons rises 22 kilometres, about two and a half Everests, and its base would cover France.

Earth is not a perfect ball either. Its spin flings the equator outward, so Earth is 43 kilometres wider across the equator than from pole to pole. The point on Earth farthest from the centre is not Everest but a volcano in Ecuador called Chimborazo.
pages.cap: Gravity squeezes a big planet into a ball and sorts it into layers, heaviest at the centre.

pages.h: Gravity built everything you can see
p: Just after the Big Bang the universe was almost perfectly smooth, a thin fog of hydrogen and helium with differences in density of only one part in 100,000. Gravity grabbed those tiny differences and amplified them. Slightly denser spots pulled in more gas, got denser, pulled harder. Over a few hundred million years the fog collapsed into clumps, and the clumps became the first stars and galaxies.

Inside a collapsing cloud, gravity squeezes gas until it heats up. At the centre of the Sun the squeeze has reached 15 million degrees Celsius and a pressure 250 billion times that of air at sea level. That is hot enough for hydrogen nuclei to fuse into helium and release energy. The outward push of that energy exactly balances gravity's inward pull. A star is a tug of war that lasts billions of years.

When the fuel runs out, gravity wins. A star like the Sun shrinks to a white dwarf the size of Earth. A heavier star collapses in less than a second to a neutron star, a city-sized ball so dense that a teaspoon of it would weigh a billion tonnes. The heaviest collapse all the way to black holes. Gravity lit the stars, and gravity puts them out.
pages.cap: Gravity pulls gas into stars. When a big star dies, gravity crushes its core in less than a second.

pages.h: Galaxies spin too fast: dark matter
p: In the 1970s an astronomer named Vera Rubin measured how fast stars orbit at the edges of galaxies. By Newton's and Einstein's rules, the outer stars, far from most of the galaxy's visible mass, should move slowly, the way Neptune moves more slowly than Mercury. They did not. Stars at the edge moved just as fast as stars near the middle.

There are two ways to read this. Either the law of gravity is wrong at large distances, or there is far more mass out there than we can see. Most physicists favour the second, because the extra mass also shows up in bent light, in the way galaxies cluster, and in the leftover glow of the Big Bang. The invisible stuff is called dark matter. It seems to outweigh ordinary matter about five to one.

Nobody knows what it is. It does not give off light, absorb light or bump into anything. Deep underground detectors have searched for its particles for 30 years and found nothing. A minority of scientists still argue that modifying gravity is the better answer, and so far neither side has won. Most of the gravity in the universe comes from something we have never touched.
pages.cap: The visible stars of a spiral galaxy sit inside a much larger, invisible halo that holds them together.

pages.h: The universe is speeding up: dark energy
p: Gravity pulls things together, so the expansion of the universe that began with the Big Bang should be slowing down. In 1998 two teams set out to measure how much it had slowed, using exploding stars as distance markers. The answer made no sense: the expansion is speeding up. Something is pushing space apart, harder and harder. The three leaders won the Nobel Prize in 2011.

Scientists named the push dark energy, which is an honest way of saying 'we do not know'. In the current best model, dark energy makes up about 68 percent of everything in the universe. Dark matter is about 27 percent. The ordinary atoms that make stars, planets and you are the remaining 5 percent.

The simplest explanation is that empty space itself has a tiny energy that pushes outward. But when physicists try to calculate how big that energy should be, they get a number too large by a factor of 10 followed by 120 zeros, the worst prediction in the history of science. In 2024 and 2025 a survey called DESI found hints that dark energy may be weakening over time, which the simplest model forbids. Scientists are arguing about it right now. This chapter may be out of date by the time you read it, and that is a good thing.
pages.cap: Space has been expanding since the Big Bang. For the last 5 billion years the expansion has been speeding up.

pages.h: Gravity is the weakest force there is
p: A fridge magnet the size of a coin can hold up a paper clip against the pull of the entire planet. Between two protons, electric force beats gravity by a factor of 10 followed by 36 zeros. Nobody knows why gravity is so feeble.

pages.h: Where Einstein and the quantum do not agree
p: Physics has two great theories. General relativity describes gravity, planets, stars and the whole universe, and it is smooth and predictable. Quantum mechanics describes atoms, light and particles, and it is jumpy, grainy and based on chance. Each has passed every test. And they do not fit together.

Most of the time that does not matter, because big things are not quantum and small things barely have gravity. But at the centre of a black hole, and at the first instant of the Big Bang, enormous mass is packed into a tiny space. Both theories apply at once. Plug the numbers in and the equations give infinities, which is mathematics for 'this is nonsense'. A point of infinite density, called a singularity, is almost certainly a sign that the theory has broken, not a real thing.

Physicists have spent 50 years trying to build a quantum theory of gravity. String theory says particles are tiny vibrating strings in extra dimensions. Loop quantum gravity says space itself comes in tiny grains. Neither has made a prediction that an experiment can check. Scientists argue, sometimes sharply, about which is on the right track, and whether either is. It is one of the biggest open problems in science, and it is wide open.
pages.cap: An atom follows quantum rules. A planet follows Einstein's rules. Nobody has one set of rules that works for both.

pages.h: What we still do not know
p: Here is an honest list of gravity questions that no one on Earth can answer yet.

What is inside a black hole? The equations say a singularity, but that probably means the equations have failed. In 1974 Stephen Hawking showed black holes should slowly leak energy and eventually evaporate. For a black hole with the Sun's mass that would take 10 followed by 67 zeros years, so none has evaporated yet. Worse, his result seems to erase information about what fell in, which the quantum rules forbid. This 'information paradox' has been argued over for 50 years. Progress since 2019 suggests the information does escape, but how is still unclear.
Does gravity come in particles? Every other force does. The guessed particle is called the graviton. Nobody has detected one, and a detector that could would need to be the mass of Jupiter.
Why is gravity so weak compared with other forces? Does it leak into extra dimensions? Why is the universe speeding up? Is dark matter a particle or a flaw in the law?
Every one of these questions is open for anyone willing to learn the mathematics. Newton was 23 when he had the idea about the Moon. Someone reading this book will be the right age at the right time.
pages.cap: Before the Big Bang, inside a black hole, between the quantum and the cosmos: the map still has blank spaces.

items: acceleration
how quickly speed changes; near Earth, falling things gain 9.8 m/s every second
mass
the amount of stuff in an object, in kilograms; the same everywhere
weight
the force gravity pulls on a mass; it changes from planet to planet
orbit
the path of something falling around a bigger object and always missing
inverse square law
double the distance and the pull drops to a quarter
spacetime
space and time treated as one four-dimensional shape that mass can bend
event horizon
the boundary of a black hole; nothing inside can get out
gravitational wave
a ripple in spacetime made by moving masses, first detected in 2015
dark matter
invisible mass that outweighs ordinary matter about five to one; nobody knows what it is
dark energy
the unknown push that makes the universe expand faster and faster
singularity
a point where the equations give infinite density; probably a sign the theory has broken

qs: Newton's law was 'wrong' in a tiny way that took 200 years to notice. Does that make it a bad theory? What would it take for Einstein's theory to be 'wrong' in the same way?
If gravity makes time run slower near heavy things, is there any place in the universe where time runs 'correctly'? What would that even mean?
Dark matter has never been detected directly. At what point should scientists give up on it and change the law of gravity instead? How would you decide?
